questions.text: Consider the queues Q1 containing four elements and Q2 containing none (shown as the Initial State in the figure). The only operations allowed on these two queues are [latex]Enqueue(Q,element)[/latex] and [latex]Dequeue(Q)[/latex]. The minimum number of [latex]Enqueue [/latex] operations on Q1 required to place the elements of Q1 in Q2 in reverse order (shown as the Final State in the figure) without using any additional storage is
questions.solution:
Use only Q2 for the reversal: after enqueueing each new element into Q2, rotate the older elements behind it (dequeue from Q2 and enqueue into Q2).
- Move 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q2: [1]
- Move 2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q2: [1, 2], rotate once [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [2, 1]
- Move 3 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q2, rotate twice [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [3, 2, 1]
- Move 4 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q2, rotate 3 times [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [4, 3, 2, 1]

Q1 is only dequeued, never enqueued.

Answer: 0

questions.text: Suppose a binary search tree with 1000 distinct elements is also a complete binary tree. The tree is stored using the array representation of binary heap trees. Assuming that the array indices start with 0, the 3rd largest element of the tree is stored at index _______.
questions.solution:
Complete tree with 1000 nodes (indices 0-999). Children of i: [latex]2i+1[/latex], [latex]2i+2[/latex].

- Largest = go right as far as possible: 0 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 6 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 14 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 30 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 62 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 126 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 254 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 510. Its children 1021, 1022 do not exist, so index 510 is the largest.
- 2nd largest = predecessor of 510. It has no left child, so it is its parent: index 254.
- 3rd largest = maximum of the left subtree of 254. Left child = 509; its children 1019, 1020 do not exist, so it is 509.

Answer: 509

questions.text:
Suppose we are given [latex]n[/latex] keys, [latex]m[/latex] hash table slots, and two simple uniform hash functions [latex]h_1[/latex] and [latex]h_2[/latex]. Further suppose our hashing scheme uses [latex]h_1[/latex] for the odd keys
and [latex]h_2[/latex] for the even keys. What is the expected number of keys in a slot?
questions.solution:
Both [latex]h_1[/latex] and [latex]h_2[/latex] are simple uniform hash functions, so every key (odd or even) lands in any given slot with probability [latex]\frac{1}{m}[/latex].

Expected keys in a slot [latex]=n\times\frac{1}{m}=\frac{n}{m}[/latex] (which hash function is used does not matter).

Answer: [latex]\frac{n}{m}[/latex]

questions.text:
Consider the problem of reversing a singly linked list. To take an example, given the linked list below,

the reversed linked list should look like

Which one of the following statements is TRUE about the time complexity of algorithms that solve the above problem in O(1) space?
questions.solution:
Walk the list once with three pointers (prev, curr, next), reversing each link as you go:
next = curr[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]next; curr[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next.

Each node is visited once and only 3 extra pointers are used, so it takes [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] time in [latex]O(1)[/latex] space. It cannot be faster, because every link must be changed.

Answer: The best algorithm takes [latex]\theta(n)[/latex] time in the worst case
